title: Why scale destroys most creative ideas
dek: The problem is not that campaigns get scaled. It is that scale is treated as a production task rather than a creative one.

body.v: There is a familiar shape to the failure. A team develops a strong idea, produces a hero film that everyone is proud of, and then hands the idea to a scaling process. Six weeks later there are four hundred assets and the idea is gone.
Nobody decided to destroy it. The destruction is procedural.
Scale is usually briefed as coverage

When scale is briefed as coverage, the unit of measurement is the format list: how many placements, how many crops, how many durations, how many markets. The question being answered is whether the campaign is present. Nobody is asked whether it is still recognisable.

So each asset is produced against the format rather than against the idea, and every one of them is a slightly weaker restatement of the original. The hero film contains the whole thought. The fifteen-second cutdown contains most of it. The six-second bumper contains a logo and a colour.
A campaign that is 90% as good four hundred times is not a strong campaign. It is a slow erosion with a media plan attached.
The alternative is to design the rules before the assets

Ideas that survive scale tend to have something in common: somebody decided, in advance, which elements were fixed and which were free. Not as a brand guideline written after the fact, but as a creative decision made while the idea was still being formed.

Fixed might be a single compositional rule, a sound, a piece of grammar, a colour used exactly once. Free might be everything else. The constraint is what makes the two-hundredth asset recognisable as a member of the same family rather than a survivor of the same brief.
Compounding, not coverage
The test we apply is simple. If someone sees only the fourth-tier asset — the vertical cutdown on a small screen with the sound off — do they receive the idea, or do they receive an advertisement?
If it is the latter, the scale plan is spending money to make the campaign smaller.

title: Luxury brands do not have a content problem
dek: Volume is the easiest thing in the world to buy. Meaning is the constraint, and it has always been the constraint.

body.v: Ask most premium brands what is holding their marketing back and the answer will be capacity. Not enough assets, not enough formats, not enough velocity. It is a comfortable answer because it can be solved with budget.
It is also, in our experience, almost never the actual problem.
The audit that changes the conversation
Lay out twelve months of a brand's output and ask a single question of each item: what does this make someone believe that they did not believe before seeing it?
Most of it will not survive the question. Not because the work is bad — much of it is well made — but because it was commissioned to fill a slot rather than to move a belief.
Brands publish more than ever. People remember less. The two facts are related.
Why this is worse for luxury

A mass brand can survive on availability. Being present at the moment of purchase is a large part of the job. A luxury brand cannot, because it is not competing to be chosen at the shelf. It is competing to be desired in advance, often for years.
Desire does not accumulate through frequency. It accumulates through specificity — one thing said well enough that it is still being repeated later.
What to do instead

Reduce the calendar. Spend the recovered budget on fewer, better ideas and on the production quality that makes them credible. Then scale those ideas properly, which is a different discipline from producing more.
This is an unpopular recommendation because it makes the marketing function look less busy. It is also, almost always, the one that shows up in brand tracking.

title: The economics of desire
dek: Restraint is not a style preference. It is a pricing strategy that happens to look like taste.

body.v: Every premium brand is running the same equation, whether or not anyone writes it down. Price is sustained by the gap between what something costs to make and what it means to own. Marketing either widens that gap or closes it.
Most communication closes the gap

Explanation closes it. Justification closes it. Volume closes it fastest of all, because ubiquity is the opposite of scarcity and audiences read availability as a signal about value long before they read the copy.
This is why discounting damages a luxury brand more than the margin loss suggests. The discount is not the problem. The disclosure is: it reveals that the price was a position rather than a fact.
What widens it

Consistency over long horizons. Craft that is visible without being announced. Restraint — specifically, the decision to say less than you could, which reads as confidence because it is expensive to sustain.
The colour used once is worth more than the colour used everywhere, and it costs less.
Restraint compounds

A brand that repeats a small number of signals with discipline builds recognition that cannot be bought quickly by a competitor. That is a durable asset and it appears on the balance sheet eventually, under a heading nobody in the creative department gets to see.

The reason so few brands do it is not that the strategy is difficult to understand. It is that it requires saying no to work that would have been perfectly acceptable, quarter after quarter, in front of people who are measured on activity.
